-----

The following code chunk will:

(a) load the "ggplot2", "gridExtra" and "knitr" packages, assuming each has been installed on your machine,
(b) read-in the abalones dataset, defining a new data frame, "mydata,"
(c) return the structure of that data frame, and
(d) calculate new variables, VOLUME and RATIO.

Do not include package installation code in this document. Packages should be installed via the Console or 'Packages' tab. You will also need to download the abalones.csv from the course site to a known location on your machine. Unless a *file.path()* is specified, R will look to directory where this .Rmd is stored when knitting.

```{r analysis_setup1, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}

# a) Load the ggplot2 and gridExtra packages.

library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(knitr)

# b) Use read.csv() to read the abalones.csv into R, assigning the data frame to "mydata."

mydata <- read.csv("abalones.csv", sep = ",", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)


# c) Use the str() function to verify the structure of "mydata." You should have 1036 observations
# of eight variables.

str(mydata)

# d) Define two new variables, VOLUME and RATIO. Use the following statements to define VOLUME and
# RATIO as variables appended to the data frame "mydata."

mydata$VOLUME <- mydata$LENGTH * mydata$DIAM * mydata$HEIGHT
mydata$RATIO <- mydata$SHUCK / mydata$VOLUME

```

### Test Items starts from here - There are 6 sections - Total 50 points

***##### Section 1: (6 points) Summarizing the data.***

(1)(a) (1 point) Use *summary()* to obtain and present descriptive statistics from mydata.  Use *table()* to present a frequency table using CLASS and RINGS. There should be 115 cells in the table you present.  

```{r Part_1a}
summary(mydata)
(table(mydata$CLASS,mydata$RINGS))

```

**Question (1 point):  Briefly discuss the variable types and distributional implications such as potential skewness and outliers.**

***Answer: (The set contains eight quantitative variables and two qualitative variables. The metric variables being length, diameter, height, whole, shuck, rings, volume, and ratio, and the non-metric variables being sex and class. The Whole, Volume, Shuck, and Rings variables contain maximum values which will potentially skew the data. As the range of these variables contain maximum values significantly above the 3rd quartile, the computation would produce values which affect the mean. Therefore, the median will be a better measurement to examine the interquartile range.)***

(1)(b) (1 point) Generate a table of counts using SEX and CLASS. Add margins to this table (Hint: There should be 15 cells in this table plus the marginal totals. Apply *table()* first, then pass the table object to *addmargins()* (Kabacoff Section 7.2 pages 144-147)).  Lastly, present a barplot of these data; ignoring the marginal totals.  

```{r Part_1b}
library(RColorBrewer)
sex_class <- table(mydata$SEX,mydata$CLASS)
addmargins(sex_class) 
coul <- brewer.pal(3, "Set1")
barplot(height = table(mydata$SEX,mydata$CLASS), col = coul, beside = TRUE) 

```

**Essay Question (2 points):  Discuss the sex distribution of abalones.  What stands out about the distribution of abalones by CLASS?**

***Answer: (The barplot visualizes the distribution by sex and class of the abalones dataset. Classes A1 and A2 have the highest count of infant abalones. Class A3 has approximately half the total of infants compared to the infant values of class A1. While classes A4 and A5 have approximately half the values of class A3. Notably, A4 and A5 approximate the infant values of one another's class. The lowest adult sex-counts of male and female abalones are found in A1 with an increase in A2, and peak counts in A3. These adult sex-counts drop in class A4, and again in A5. However, the lowered adult sex-counts in A5 compared to A4 show both classes share approximate values of sex-counts.)***

(1)(c) (1 point) Select a simple random sample of 200 observations from "mydata" and identify this sample as "work." Use *set.seed(123)* prior to drawing this sample. Do not change the number 123. Note that *sample()* "takes a sample of the specified size from the elements of x." We cannot sample directly from "mydata." Instead, we need to sample from the integers, 1 to 1036, representing the rows of "mydata." Then, select those rows from the data frame (Kabacoff Section 4.10.5 page 87). 

Using "work", construct a scatterplot matrix of variables 2-6 with *plot(work[, 2:6])* (these are the continuous variables excluding VOLUME and RATIO). The sample "work" will not be used in the remainder of the assignment. 

```{r Part_1c}
set.seed(123)
work <- mydata[sample(x = 1:nrow(mydata), size = 200, replace = FALSE),]
str(work)
plot(work[, 2:6],)
```

***##### Section 2: (5 points) Summarizing the data using graphics.***

(2)(a) (1 point) Use "mydata" to plot WHOLE versus VOLUME. Color code data points by CLASS.

```{r Part_2a}
ggplot(data = mydata, aes(x=VOLUME, y=WHOLE, color=CLASS)) + geom_point() + 
  scale_color_manual(labels = levels(factor(mydata$CLASS)),
                        values = c("orange", "red", "green", "black", "blue"))

                        

```


(2)(b) (2 points) Use "mydata" to plot SHUCK versus WHOLE with WHOLE on the horizontal axis. Color code data points by CLASS. As an aid to interpretation, determine the maximum value of the ratio of SHUCK to WHOLE.  Add to the chart a straight line with zero intercept using this maximum value as the slope of the line. If you are using the 'base R' *plot()* function, you may use *abline()* to add this line to the plot. Use *help(abline)* in R to determine the coding for the slope and intercept arguments in the functions. If you are using ggplot2 for visualizations, *geom_abline()* should be used.

```{r Part_2b}
ggplot(data = mydata, aes(x=WHOLE, y=SHUCK, color=CLASS)) + geom_point() + geom_abline(slope = max(mydata$SHUCK / mydata$WHOLE), intercept = 0) + ggtitle("Shuck weight, in grams | Whole weight, in grams") +
  xlab("Whole weight") + ylab("Shuck weight") + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) +
  scale_color_manual(labels = levels(factor(mydata$CLASS)),
                        values = c("orange", "red", "green", "black", "blue")) 
  
 
```

**Essay Question (2 points):  How does the variability in this plot differ from the plot in (a)?  Compare the two displays.  Keep in mind that SHUCK is a part of WHOLE.  Consider the location of the different age classes.**

***Answer: (The x-axis measures volume and y-axis measures whole weight in plot A. The x-axis measures whole weight and the y-axis measure shuck weight in plot B. Plot B has data with less variability between the data points as a result of the measurement variables on the axes. Class A1 on plot A displays the highest variability between 125 and 250 along the volume axis. However, plot B displays the highest variability between 50 and 100 along the whole weight axis. Therefore, plot B contains less outlier values for class A1 than plot A. Classes A3, A4, and A5 have more outlier values in plot A than in plot B. Class A5 has the highest variability across both plots. What is seen in both plots is increased weight and volume occurring in classes A3, A4, and A5. This is expected as age and weight share a positive correlation.)***

(3)(b) (2 points) The boxplots in (3)(a) indicate that there are outlying RATIOs for each sex. *boxplot.stats()* can be used to identify outlying values of a vector. Present the abalones with these outlying RATIO values along with their associated variables in "mydata". Display the observations by passing a data frame to the kable() function. Basically, we want to output those rows of "mydata" with an outlying RATIO, but we want to determine outliers looking separately at infants, females and males.

```{r Part_3b}
fml_out <- boxplot.stats(x = mydata[mydata$SEX =="F", "RATIO"])$out
inf_out <- boxplot.stats(x = mydata[mydata$SEX =="I", "RATIO"])$out
ml_out <- boxplot.stats(x = mydata[mydata$SEX =="M", "RATIO"])$out
fml_df <- mydata[mydata$SEX == "F" & mydata$RATIO %in% fml_out,]
inf_df <- mydata[mydata$SEX =="I" & mydata$RATIO %in% inf_out,] 
ml_df <- mydata[mydata$SEX == "M" & mydata$RATIO %in% ml_out,] 
total_df <- rbind(fml_df, inf_df, ml_df)
kable(total_df)
```

**Essay Question (2 points):  What are your observations regarding the results in (3)(b)?**

***Answer: (Infant abalones have the highest counts of outliers compared to the outlier counts of both male abalones and female abalones. Classes A1 and A2 contain the highest outlier counts for infant abalones. For females, classes A2, A3, and A5 have the outlier counts. For males, outlier counts are found in clas A3. )***

***### Section 5: (12 points) Getting insights regarding different groups in the data.***

(5)(a) (2 points) Use *aggregate()* with "mydata" to compute the mean values of VOLUME, SHUCK and RATIO for each combination of SEX and CLASS. Then, using *matrix()*, create matrices of the mean values. Using the "dimnames" argument within *matrix()* or the *rownames()* and *colnames()* functions on the matrices, label the rows by SEX and columns by CLASS. Present the three matrices (Kabacoff Section 5.6.2, p. 110-111). The *kable()* function is useful for this purpose.  You do not need to be concerned with the number of digits presented.

```{r Part_5a}
mean_vol <- aggregate(VOLUME ~ SEX + CLASS, data = mydata, FUN = mean)
vol_mat <- matrix(data = round(mean_vol$VOLUME, 3), nrow = 3, byrow = FALSE, 
                  dimnames = list(c("Female", "Infant", "Male"), levels(mydata$CLASS)))
mean_shk <- aggregate(SHUCK ~ SEX + CLASS, data = mydata, FUN = mean)
shk_mat <- matrix(data = round(mean_shk$SHUCK, 3), nrow = 3, byrow = FALSE, 
                  dimnames = list(c("Female", "Infant", "Male"), levels(mydata$CLASS)))
mean_rt <- aggregate(RATIO ~ SEX + CLASS, data = mydata, FUN = mean)
rt_mat <- matrix(data = round(mean_rt$RATIO, 3), nrow = 3, byrow = FALSE, 
                  dimnames = list(c("Female", "Infant", "Male"), levels(mydata$CLASS)))
 
kable(vol_mat, caption = "Volume")
kable(shk_mat, caption = "Shuck")
kable(rt_mat, caption = "Ratio") 
```

(5)(b) (3 points) Present three graphs. Each graph should include three lines, one for each sex. The first should show mean RATIO versus CLASS; the second, mean VOLUME versus CLASS; the third, mean SHUCK versus CLASS. This may be done with the 'base R' *interaction.plot()* function or with ggplot2 using *grid.arrange()*.

```{r Part_5b, fig.width = 9}
interaction.plot(x.factor = mydata$CLASS, trace.factor = mydata$SEX,
                 response = mydata$RATIO, fun = mean, xlab= "Class", ylab = "Ratio", col = palette()) 
interaction.plot(x.factor = mydata$CLASS, trace.factor = mydata$SEX,
                 response = mydata$VOLUME, fun = mean, xlab= "Class", ylab = "Volume", col = palette()) 
interaction.plot(x.factor = mydata$CLASS, trace.factor = mydata$SEX,
                 response = mydata$SHUCK, fun = mean, xlab= "Class", ylab = "Shuck", col = palette()) 
```

5(c) (3 points) Present four boxplots using *par(mfrow = c(2, 2)* or *grid.arrange()*. ```{r Part_5c}


**Essay Question (2 points):  What do these displays suggest about abalone growth?  Also, compare the infant and adult displays.  What differences stand out?**

***Answer: (As abalones age, the rate of increasing volume begins to decrease. Thus the dataset shows an abalone reaching its maximum volume in adulthood. There is more variability occurring in the infant graphs. Additionally, more outlier values are found in infants who have between eight to eleven rings. Variability for adults begins to occur for groups with rings between seven and eleven. Also, volume and weight increase with increased ring counts.)***

***### Section 6: (11 points) Conclusions from the Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA).***


**Conclusions**


**Essay Question 1) (5 points)	Based solely on these data, what are plausible statistical reasons that explain the failure of the original study? Consider to what extent physical measurements may be used for age prediction.**

***Answer: (Outliers affected the final analysis as a result of these not having been addressed prior to beginning the study. This impacted achieving normal distribution of the data and skewed the data toward the right. With the highest counts of outliers contained the infant class, the categorization of sexes should be addressed to ensure standardization is consistent to prevent incorrect categorization. Of note, the only group found in all five categories was the infants. This potentially could have occurred as a result of relying on different variables at each instance of classification. The mean ratio, volume, and shuck are valid measurements producing higher reliability in determining the approximate age of abalones when compared to solely rings. Environmental factors were also not included in the dataset. Geographic location, water temperature, water levels, local pollution, predators, food, and other factors which could potentially impact growth, sex populations, and count values across all classes.)***

**Essay Question 2) (3 points) Do not refer to the abalone data or study.  If you were presented with an overall histogram and summary statistics from a sample of some population or phenomenon and no other information, what questions might you ask before accepting them as representative of the sampled population or phenomenon?**

***Answer: (I would inquire about the collection of the data, the quality of the data, and control of the data. I would need to determine is the sample collected occurred from the same geographic region, in addition to further investigating what tools and method were utilized to collect the data. This would impact the quality of the data if uniform practices were not followed during this task. Potentially comparing data points from different sources within one variable. The analysis would be corrupted, producing inconclusive results. I would want to look at measures of central tendency, in addition to the following: standard deviation of the distribution, and data symmetry. Again, the mean and median values are impacted by poor data collection, quality, and control. The result being poor decision-making and hampered strategic execution.)***

**Essay Question 3)  (3 points)	Do not refer to the abalone data or study.  What do you see as difficulties analyzing data derived from observational studies? Can causality be determined?  What might be learned from such studies?**

***Answer: (Observational studies are susceptible to human error. Bias can potentially affect recording of data and therefore produce incorrect correlation relationships which is not representative of real World phenomena. Measures values would not be true values. Assumed values would create a barrier in obtaining valid and reliable results from the data. Thus, causality is a characteristic of the observer's bias. This would impact causality since the quality and control of data have poorly established definitions of qualitative and quantitative attributes of the data. Things which could be learned is how the research was designed and also its implementation. The design would provide insight into determining and defining if the appropriate problem was correctly stated. The implementation would provide insight into methods and tools and wheter these are effective for such a study.)***
